text: Kristóf Szabó aka KristofLab presents his most critical project yet, Artificial Paradise. His practice explores the relationship between nature and civilisation, wilderness and urbanisation, and man's artificially created habitat: the city and its symbol, the tower block.

Artificial Paradise takes this further: artificially created natural spaces, domesticated and industrialised nature. Visions of the future that seemed utopian a few decades ago (a new relationship between nature and man, the possibility of total control) have become everyday practice.

Controlled, industrialised nature calls into question the very definition of nature. Can we still speak of nature when vegetation is artificially created and sustained, and functions as a visual element? How does this affect ecology and our image of nature?

KristofLab uses his usual multimedia tools (installations, videos, paintings and collages) to explore the bizarre, alienating nature of the phenomenon, and to envision the possibilities encoded in its present.
textCredit: Text by Luca Cserhalmi, esthete, curator of the exhibition. The exhibition was opened by Barnabás Zemlényi-Kovács, theorist and independent curator.

behindTheScenes: The floor plan is traced from the gallery's own room sheet and its overall length matches the building's outline on OpenStreetMap. Rooms are measured from 360° panorama photos: solving the camera position from the corners and the four canvases of known size gives the room's real size, the recess around the doorway and where the windows, the screen and the plant stood. Every painting hangs at its listed canvas size and measured height. The brick on the walls is cut from the photographs: a script measures the 7.7 cm brick courses for scale, divides out the gallery lighting and stitches each patch so it tiles along the mortar joints. The paintings and prints are the artist’s own reproductions, and the screens play the artist's videos with their own sound. Paradise Factory and the plastic river of Let it Flow are modelled from the photos. Three.js and Vite, no backend; the room tone is synthesised with Web Audio.

human-as-error.heading: About the series
text: Humanity has been on Earth for only about 300,000 years, while life emerged around 3.5 million years ago. Our species began to transform the planet more drastically around the time of the Industrial Revolution, and a large share of these processes falls within the last 70 years.

We can think of ourselves as an error with regard to natural diversity. Looking at the past century, it is no exaggeration to estimate a decline of two thirds. There have been 5 great mass extinctions in the history of the Earth so far, each reaching 75%. According to the Red List of the IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature), over the past 100 years roughly 27% of currently known species have become threatened or endangered with extinction: among them 25% of mammals, 13% of birds, 41% of amphibians and 33% of plants.

The settlement chosen as the subject of the series, Szentkirályszabadja near Veszprém, was a Russian military base and barracks that emptied after the change of regime. Nature has already brought its human-built structures under its rule. Working with these images, I deal conceptually with the disappearance of humans from nature. It takes only decades for nature to take back the domesticated landscape and for biodiversity to return. The depopulation of settlements is not the result of planned events; it can be put down to chance, with human activities among its causes. Error and its aesthetics hold a key place, and this is reflected in the pictures as well: chance plays a large part in my painting method, and I build up the glitched surfaces with abstracted brushwork.

In this series my aim is to rethink landscape painting. Nature reconquers what humans took from it, the “original” state returns, and we can once again admire its grandeur and strength, which also shows its power towering above civilisation. What connects most closely with my work is the aesthetic of ruins, and the love of them, in the painting of Caspar David Friedrich. A similar line of thought runs through both: in each case the dominion of nature towers above human activity. It reconquers what humans took. In Friedrich’s lifetime industrialisation completely transformed the world; today we are living through its culmination. Capitalism has turned even nature into a commodity. In Friedrich’s work the sublimity of nature can also signify a longing for an age when civilisation still lived in symbiosis with it. In my work the concept of humans subordinated to nature appears, so the built environment slowly turns into ruins, only hinting at the former “glory” of our civilisation.
human-as-error.note: Translated from the artist’s Hungarian text for the digital exhibition.

landscape.heading: About the series
text: The theme of the series is the relationship between man and his environment in the light of capitalism. The harmonious fusion of the urban and the natural environment seems utopian in this context. In the existing system, the crossing of boundaries can have two extreme consequences. On the positive side, pushing boundaries can lead to progress, which can lead to development. Negatively: by crossing the boundary, we can set in motion irreversible processes with uncertain outcomes.

paradise-factory.heading: About the work
text: Paradise Factory explores new yet increasingly familiar configurations of the relationship between nature and civilization. Through rapid technological advancement and industrialization, the hierarchy between humans and nature has deepened—manifesting in altered landscapes, artificially sustained urban vegetation, and food crops grown entirely without sunlight in closed systems. The installation features a hydroponic cultivation setup alongside a repurposed monitor displaying manipulated footage of the growing process. This ambivalent assemblage simultaneously questions and reflects on emerging nature-constructs that, in an era of climate change, soil degradation, and food insecurity, may soon become the norm. At its core, the work poses a pressing question: where do we draw the line between the natural and the artificial today—and what do we even mean by "nature"?

let-it-flow.heading: About the work
text: Let it Flow is a site-specific installation that examines the disrupted material flows between humans and nature through the lens of recycling and object cultures created from waste. The work is composed partly of plastic waste collected from the River Tisza during the river-cleaning actions of the PET Kupa, and partly of plastic remnants generated within the artist’s own household.

The assemblage is built upon the duality of “flow” and “waste circulation”: the Tisza as a natural watercourse and plastic as an artificially produced yet now uncontrollable material process become layered onto one another. Waste does not disappear; instead, it searches for a new form. Through melting with a heat gun, the found objects partially lose their original function while entering a new, transitional plastic state. In this way, “useless” materials are reinterpreted as artworks.

Let it Flow is therefore not merely an installation, but a visual protocol following cycles of material circulation: a recontextualization of objects originating from pollution, in which the boundaries between natural and artificial systems become increasingly blurred.

openingSpeech.author: Barnabás Zemlényi-Kovács
openingSpeech.title: Opening speech for Kristóf Szabó's exhibition Artificial Paradise
openingSpeech.note: Translated from the Hungarian original for the digital exhibition.
text: 165 years ago two men, both forty years old and knowing nothing of each other, one in France and the other in Ireland, each wrote a long study about smoke. It may sound surprising, but in my view Kristóf Szabó's exhibition can be placed somewhere in the connections between these two texts, both written around 1860 and, despite their related subject, seemingly very far apart. One of the men was John Tyndall, an Irish physicist who in 1859 began experiments to measure with laboratory instruments how effectively various gases, such as carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane, hold on to heat. Tyndall was thus the first to prove that certain components of the atmosphere, carbon dioxide above all, absorb and re-radiate a large part of the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth, and so warm the atmosphere. Tyndall's discovery is nothing other than what we now call the greenhouse effect. The Irish physicist carried out his research at the dawn of the second industrial revolution, that is, precisely when human activity began to drive up the concentration of carbon dioxide, which, through the greenhouse effect Tyndall described, led to global warming and to the climate crisis of our time.

If Tyndall's problem was that smoke, in a sense, stays, the other author's was precisely that it inevitably drifts away. In 1860 Charles Baudelaire published his study Artificial Paradises: for him the term, which also gives this exhibition its title, means the alternative wish-realities and ephemeral utopias induced by intoxicants such as hashish and opium. In this personal text, which largely reflects on his own drug use, Baudelaire circles the fundamental ambivalence of this intoxicated happiness and psychedelic fantasy world: unlike real social movements, this state can offer only a passing salvation, and once the drug wears off the user falls back into a bare reality that seems all the more desolate. In other words, only one step separates the artificial paradise from a real hell.

In Kristóf Szabó's works these two texts, written 165 years ago, are fused: his exhibition is filled with gigantic greenhouses built in response to global warming, mini-ecospheres designed to be sustainable, artificially created micro-Edens, or, as he himself calls them, “artificial paradises”. All of these are at once concrete scientific and technological answers to the climate situation, metaphors that point far beyond themselves, and utopias or wish-images of a sustainable future. And here it turns out that Baudelaire is present far beyond the title: although they are indeed more environmentally friendly than today's agricultural mass production, in Kristóf Szabó's exhibition these utopian “artificial natures”, just like Baudelaire's artificial paradises, are unmasked as fantasies whose sustainability is more than questionable, and which, as apparent answers to the crisis, partly seem to cover up the real questions.

John Tyndall did not yet use the greenhouse metaphor for greenhouse gases; it was introduced by the Swede Nils Ekholm in 1901. The artificial ecospheres Kristóf Szabó examines are built precisely on the greenhouse, which holds a certain dark irony, since they appear as a response to a climate crisis in which the whole planet has turned into an overheated global greenhouse. The greenhouse, the archetype of the artificial, humanly controlled environment, goes back to antiquity; the Romans already experimented with it. The greenhouse is an ecological paradox in which nature is the more ideal, the more artificial the conditions it is created in. Where nature is artificial, the artificial is natural. This ideal, seemingly untouched environment, which also appears in documentary footage in Kristóf Szabó's works, is made possible by an all-encompassing human control, that is, by the same logic that led to the present situation.

Baudelaire was not only one of the most influential, proto-avant-garde poets of his time but also a defining art critic and theorist of the period, one of the first to formulate the intellectual foundations of the emerging modern art. In 1863, two years after Artificial Paradises, Baudelaire wrote his essay The Painter of Modern Life, perhaps the first manifesto of modern art. “The transitory, the fugitive, the contingent make up one half of art; the other half is the eternal and the immutable,” Baudelaire writes. “[The artist] is looking for that quality which we may call modernity (…) His task is to extract from fashion whatever poetry within history it may contain, to distil the eternal from the transitory.” Despite all the crises of modernity, Baudelaire's avant-garde definition of art still sets the basic frame of art today. Kristóf Szabó, too, stands with one foot in tradition and the other in the ephemeral present; it is enough to mention his conscious dialogue with the traditional genre of the landscape. In the time of Tyndall and Baudelaire, it was artists who created artificial ideal landscapes, and the exhibition also quotes these 19th-century romantic, academic or impressionist landscape ideals. What art once produced is produced today by industry and technology, and in this situation Kristóf Szabó sees one possible task of the artist in denaturalising this synthetically produced, harmonious nature: in revealing its artificiality, in the errors, glitches and blind spots of the flawlessly staged vision, which also appear as faults in the image.

Also at the turn of the 1850s and 1860s, in 1859, a third book appeared from a third gentleman, ten years older than the other two: On the Origin of Species by Charles Darwin. Kristóf Szabó approaches the origin of species from the end of species, natural selection from artificial selection. His works claim that man is not only not the crown of creation but not even the peak of evolution; in fact, an error. Human as Error. The question is what correcting this error would mean: besides the radical transformation or abolition of capitalism, posthuman and post-anthropocentric theories argue that, if we do not want to abolish ourselves, it is precisely our human-centredness that we have to overcome in order to survive.
Our problem today is still that of Baudelaire and Tyndall: the smoke of utopia drifts away, but the smoke of dystopia stays.
